newsitem.title: GERMANY: "I know my duty," says Kohl on standing again.
newsitem.headline: "I know my duty," says Kohl on standing again.

text.p: German Chancellor Helmut Kohl, who has declined to commit himself to standing again in the 1998 general election, appeared to hint on Tuesday that he might stand again, telling a party meeting that he "knew his duty".
The assembled Christian Democrat (CDU) members of parliament immediately greeted the comment with a long round of applause, participants said.

Kohl has come under pressure to give fresh impetus to his party and the coalition government, divided over major reforms to the tax and pensions systems and struggling to stem high unemployment, by saying he will stand again in October 1998.
He told his party on Tuesday that he would not let anyone force him into making a decision before he was ready.
But he added that he knew he had a responsibility to the party and the centre-right coalition, adding: "I know my duty."

Kohl, Europe's longest serving head of government, sparked the latest round of speculation 10 days ago with an interview on French television in which he said he would ponder a fresh candidacy after a European Union reform summit in June.

Many in his party were dismayed that he appeared to have introduced a fresh note of uncertainty at a time when the coalition was under more pressure than at any time since the 1994 election, and badly in need of strong leadership.

A wave of criticism from within the party at the way the reform projects were being conducted suggested to editorial writers that Kohl was losing some of his legendary grip over internal dissent, and that he might not be able to provide the authority and new ideas required.
It was unclear on Tuesday whether Kohl's comment had really brought a decision nearer.
The idea of doing his duty is one Kohl has used in the past, most recently in a weekend interview with the daily Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung.
"I know my duty and I don't need any remedial help on this," Kohl, 66 and in his 15th year in office, told the paper. "I will make my decision known...when I consider the time to be right."

Kohl, who according to the German press is sliding into his "Kanzlerdaemmerung" (Twilight of the Chancellor), has also suggested he would not try to rally his troops with a big gesture the effect of which might fade if policy successes do not follow.
Instead, CDU officials say, Kohl is betting he can first regain his public standing by pushing through the long-overdue reforms of Germany's creaking tax and pension systems.
"The chancellor is dead set on pushing through these reforms," one official said. "Everything else is speculation."
The showcase for the chancellor -- a master of "sitting out' his difficulties -- to announce his decision could be the CDU's annual congress in October.
By that time unemployment -- which leaped by a staggering half a million last month -- should have receded a little, and the reforms could have taken shape.
